newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy sees no breakthrough in Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy sees no breakthrough in Mideast summit.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk said on Monday he did not expect a breakthrough in Tuesday's peace summit between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

"We do not expect a dramatic breakthrough...but a better understanding towards the way in which Israel, Egypt, the Palestinians and the United States will continue to advance the peace process," Israel's domestic news agency Itim quoted Indyk as saying.
"We do not want failure but I caution against expections which are too high."

The summit to be held at the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh is overshadowed by entrenched differences over Jewish settlement in lands Israel occupied in 1967. The sides have shown few signs of compromise.
Mediator Egypt supports the Palestinian view that Israeli-PLO peace talks, frozen for more than two months, will only resume when Israel halts work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Netanyahu has ruled out a halt to settlement construction.

Palestinian-Israeli peacemaking ground to a halt when Netanyahu gave the green light to the settlement of Har Homa in Arab East Jerusalem in March. Israel captured the area in 1967 and later annexed it in a move not recognised internationally.

Palestinians see the work at the site they call Jabal Abu Ghneim as pre-empting final status talks on the east of the city, which they see as the capital of a future state. Israel says all of Jerusalem is its capital.
Netanyahu says talks can resume only when the PLO cracks down on militants opposed to peace.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Monday called for vigorous U.S. intervention to end the peace deadlock: "We need the United States to play a more active role very quickly," he told reporters in self-ruled Gaza.
Indyk said the peace process would move forward only when Israel and the PLO were ready.
"Its up to the parties themselves to take the steps necessary to put the process back on track. We're ready to help them but we can't do it for them," he told reporters.
